sweep_summary: Seneca (sene1264, in catalog as weight-hedged, deciding source Chafe 1967). Three works with stress in the title, all about Seneca word accent. (1) Melinger 2002 (IJAL 68) was already held by the project (MPG PuRe open copy) and was read: rule (2) p.290 restates the closure-conditioned even-syllable rule and, citing Chafe 1996/1998, reports multiple equal-pitch accents per word and pitch as the sole correlate -- this refines the catalog's 'at most one strong stress' deciding quote without displacing Chafe 1967 as primary (the rule is 'adapted from Chafe 1996'; the better first-hand update would be Chafe 1996 HNAI sketch or Chafe 2015 grammar, neither in this search of works with stress in the title's items). (2) Michelson 1983 Harvard dissertation (published 1988 as A Comparative Study of Lake-Iroquoian Accent, Kluwer): only bibliographic records reached -- Springer DOI paywalled, archive.org copy lending-only, HathiTrust search-only; not read, priority medium. new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Foster (quoting Chafe): Seneca has abandoned the Proto-Northern-Iroquoian penultimate accent entirely; accent goes on the LAST even-numbered non-final syllable that is closed, or on the last even-numbered non-final open syllable immediately followed by a closed syllable; penults have no special status; many words receive no primary accent at all, and where there is one it often falls before the antepenult. The article's own subject is Cayuga (odd/even syllable alternation, laryngeal metathesis in odd-numbered syllables), with Seneca treated only comparatively.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Seneca has no penultimate-accent rule; accent is assigned to the LAST non-final even-numbered syllable (counting from the word beginning) that is either closed, or open and immediately followed by a non-final closed syllable; unlike the other Lake-Iroquoian languages, accent and vowel length do not fall together on the same syllable except under special conditions (secs. 3.6.1.4, 3.6.2.2); vowel length is handled by separate rules (3.6.1 Penultimate Lengthening, even-syllable lengthening). A further snippet (m88_q6) shows epenthetic vowels are counted by the accent rule ('in (101) the epenthetic e in the second syllable is accented'), and another (m88_q5) that Mohawk-type, Cayuga and Seneca rules 'all.. depend on an alternating odd/even [count]' with a suggestion that the innovation arose in 'Cayuga and was borrowed by Seneca during a period of close contact' (fragmentary).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Seneca stress always falls on an even-numbered syllable (counting from the word beginning): it is assigned to the LAST non-final even-numbered CLOSED syllable of the word, where an intervocalic h or glottal stop counts as closing the preceding syllable (the fuller 5.6 formulation, of which only the tail '..[syl]lable that is followed by a nonfinal closed syllable' is visible, adds the open-even-syllable-before-a-closed-syllable case as in the 1988 book); vowel length is assigned by separate rules (retained lengthening of open penults, which need no longer be stressed, plus 'Even Syllable Length'), and a vowel lengthened by Even Syllable Length before a qualifying cluster is not thereby stressed. Cayuga and Seneca chapters rest on published sources (chiefly Chafe 1967), not the author's fieldwork (abstract).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress is visible in the preview or snippets.
new_statements.exceptions: Intervocalic h/? close the preceding syllable for the purpose of the rule; interaction cases where a penultimate vowel meets both Seneca Stress and Even Syllable Length (resolution not visible); 'an interesting development in Seneca has to do with the behaviour of clusters in the assignment of stress and vowel length' (detail not visible).

tone_statements.quote: Vowels are pronounced with either low or high pitch. High pitched (‘accented’) vowels are marked with an acute accent: gagá’da’ ‘white oak’. Long vowels may have high pitch throughout their length, as in á:hse:gë’ ‘you might see it’, or the pitch may fall, as in à:díyë’he’t ‘they should learn’, where the falling pitch is marked with a grave accent. High pitch may occur with either short or long vowels, but falling pitch occurs only with long vowels. ... a word may contain more than one accent. ... Many words contain no word-level accent at all
tone_statements.locator: p. 9, sec. 2.2; last two clauses p. 14-15, secs. 2.7.3-2.7.4
tone_statements.summary: Word-level 'accent' = high pitch, assigned by rule to even-numbered vowels in strong trochees (after Melinger 2002); words may carry several accents or none; first and last vowels exempt; falling pitch on long vowels from leftward accent spread. Never says tone or stress. Fig. 2.1 is a pitch track.

sources.quote: 4.4. ... A basically strong vowel occurs with strong stress if it is both even and prefinal: ?akyéhtah I've hit it. If the prefinal vowel of a word is either odd or basically weak, and thus occurs with weak stress, strong stress occurs on the nearest preceding even vowel that either is basically strong itself (hoyéhta:otye?s he keeps hitting it), or has somewhere following it (but before any even prefinal vowel if there is one) either (a) a basically strong vowel, (b) a laryngeal obstruent, (c) a cluster of any two obstruents, or (d) s plus n or w. ... No word has more than one strong stress, and many words have none; e.g. hatiwenotatye?s the thunderers, hoyetota:?toh he's shaking the wood. Note in the last example that ? follows an even prefinal vowel and does not, therefore, condition a strong stress. [fn. 26 to (d): Or y in a few morphemes.]

tone.quote: Vowels are pronounced with either low or high pitch. High pitched (‘accented’) vowels are marked with an acute accent: gagá’da’ ‘white oak’. Long vowels may have high pitch throughout their length, as in á:hse:gë’ ‘you might see it’, or the pitch may fall, as in à:díyë’he’t ‘they should learn’, where the falling pitch is marked with a grave accent. High pitch may occur with either short or long vowels, but falling pitch occurs only with long vowels. ... a word may contain more than one accent. ... Many words contain no word-level accent at all
tone.locator: p. 9, sec. 2.2; last two clauses p. 14-15, secs. 2.7.3-2.7.4
tone.summary: Word-level 'accent' = high pitch, assigned by rule to even-numbered vowels in strong trochees (after Melinger 2002); words may carry several accents or none; first and last vowels exempt; falling pitch on long vowels from leftward accent spread. Never says tone or stress. Fig. 2.1 is a pitch track.
